title: Two promised sons
sum: Luke begins with a polished Greek preface to Theophilus, promising a careful account so that he can be sure of what he was taught. Then the style turns to the language of Israel's Scriptures. In the temple, the angel Gabriel tells the old priest Zechariah that his barren wife Elizabeth will bear a son, John, who will go ahead of the Lord in Elijah's spirit; Zechariah doubts and is struck silent. Six months later Gabriel tells Mary, a virgin in Nazareth promised to Joseph, that she will conceive by the Holy Spirit a son who will reign on David's throne forever. Mary agrees.

Mary visits Elizabeth, whose unborn child leaps for joy; Elizabeth blesses her, and Mary sings the Magnificat, praising the God who lifts the lowly and brings down the mighty. John is born and named, Zechariah's voice returns, and he sings the Benedictus, blessing God for raising up a Davidic Savior and naming his own son as the prophet who will prepare the way. The chapter's design pairs John and Jesus at every step, always with Jesus one step higher.
readings: Traditional readers take the chapter as an account resting on family memory, perhaps Mary's own (2:19, 51), which Luke, as he says in 1:1–4, gathered from those who were there. They note the accurate details of temple practice (the divisions, the lot for the incense, the hour of prayer) and the Semitic flavor of the songs. Many critical historians judge that the chapter cannot be checked against outside sources, that it is shaped closely on Old Testament birth stories, and that its core, a virginal conception and a link between John and Jesus, comes from early Christian tradition whose origin we cannot trace.

Luke tells these births as the Greek Old Testament told births: Abraham and Sarah's son in old age, Samson's and Samuel's mothers, the angel's message, the song of praise. A reader steeped in Israel's Scriptures hears the old story of God's faithfulness reaching its goal. The point is less what can be proved than what the story claims: that the God of Abraham and David is keeping his word now.

Jewish readers notice how Jewish this chapter is: a priestly couple who keep the commandments, temple prayer, circumcision on the eighth day, songs made of psalms and prophets, and hope for Israel's redemption. Nothing here sets Jesus against Judaism. The virginal conception itself was not a Jewish messianic expectation (the Hebrew of Isaiah 7:14 says "young woman"), which is one reason Jewish readers have historically not accepted it; but the hopes the songs express, mercy to Abraham, David's throne, rescue from enemies, are Israel's own.

views.H: The setting is real: Herod the Great's last years (before 4 BC), the twenty-four priestly divisions, the daily incense offering, a small Galilean village and the hill country of Judea. Whether the events can be confirmed is another matter: no outside source mentions Zechariah, Elizabeth or the annunciation. Historians who accept the chapter's core point to its restraint and Jewish color; those who doubt it point to how closely it follows Old Testament patterns.
views.C: Many scholars (Raymond Brown, Joseph Fitzmyer) think Luke composed chapters 1–2 last, and some that an earlier form of the Gospel began at 3:1, with its own dating formula; others (Paul Minear, Robert Tannehill) stress how closely chapters 1–2 are woven into the whole. Some think Luke drew on a source about John's birth from John's followers (1:5–25, 57–80) and joined it to traditions about Jesus. The songs may be earlier Jewish-Christian hymns that Luke inserted; the Magnificat and Benedictus fit their places loosely (the Benedictus could be lifted out and 1:80 would follow 1:66 smoothly). The minority view that Marcion's shorter Gospel, which lacked chapters 1–2, came before Luke is discussed in book.json.
views.L: The chapter is built as a diptych: two announcements (1:5–25; 1:26–38), joined by the meeting of the two mothers (1:39–56), then two births (1:57–80; 2:1–40). Each panel has the same parts, and each time Jesus' is greater: a barren old woman, then a virgin; a son who will be great before the Lord, then a son who will be called Son of the Most High; a father struck dumb for doubt, then a mother blessed for faith. The language of the Greek Old Testament gives the reader the sense of a story continuing from the Scriptures.
views.J: Luke opens his story of Jesus inside Israel's worship: the temple, the priesthood, the hour of prayer. Zechariah and Elizabeth are "righteous" Torah-keepers, praised, not criticized. The songs are Jewish prayers, full of the Psalms and Isaiah, and their hope is for Israel: mercy to Abraham's offspring, a king from David's house, rescue from enemies. Jewish scholars such as Amy-Jill Levine stress that Christian readers should not read later conflicts back into these chapters.
views.T: These verses gave the church some of its most used words: the Hail Mary (1:28, 42), the Magnificat at Vespers, the Benedictus at Lauds, and the Annunciation (March 25) and Visitation feasts. The ox, Luke's symbol among the four living creatures, was linked to this opening sacrifice in the temple. Catholic and Orthodox teaching draws much of its Marian doctrine from 1:28–48; Protestant readers honor Mary as the model believer who says "May it be done to me just as you have said."

deep.b:
Luke sets John and Jesus side by side, panel by panel (René Laurentin and Raymond Brown set this out in detail):

JohnJesus
ParentsOld priest and barren wife, righteous (1:5–7)Young virgin promised to a man of David's house (1:26–27)
The angelGabriel in the sanctuary (1:11–19)Gabriel in a Galilean village (1:26–28)
Fear and reassurance"Stop being afraid" (1:12–13)"Stop being afraid" (1:29–30)
The promiseGreat in the Lord's eyes; filled with the Spirit (1:15)Great; Son of the Most High; David's throne forever (1:32–33)
The question"How am I to know this?" (1:18)"How is this going to happen?" (1:34)
The signStruck mute (1:20)Elizabeth's pregnancy (1:36)
ResponseSilence (1:22)"Here is the Lord's slave" (1:38)
Birth and namingBorn, circumcised, named (1:57–63)Born, circumcised, named (2:6–7, 21)
SongBenedictus (1:68–79)Angels' Gloria, Nunc Dimittis (2:14, 29–32)
Growing up"Kept growing and getting stronger in spirit" (1:80)"Kept growing and getting stronger," "moving forward in wisdom" (2:40, 52)

The meeting of the mothers (1:39–56) joins the panels: the elder bows to the younger, and the unborn John greets the unborn Jesus.

Christians and scholars answer in several ways, often holding more than one at once.

Historical memory. The church has always read Luke 1–2 as true history. Many scholars today (for example Darrell Bock and Richard Bauckham) argue that Luke's preface claims eyewitness sources, that Mary and the family of Jesus were known in the early church (Acts 1:14), and that the chapters' Jewish detail and restraint fit an early, Palestinian origin.

Theology told as story. Raymond Brown, a Catholic scholar, concluded that the infancy stories contain historical elements (the names, Herod's reign, a virginal conception that both Matthew and Luke independently report) but are mainly Christian reflection on who Jesus is, told in the patterns of the Old Testament; much cannot be checked. Geza Vermes and Andrew Lincoln go further, reading them as theological legend.

The virginal conception. Matthew and Luke tell very different stories but agree on this point, which suggests the belief is older than both. Christians confess it in the creeds; most Jewish readers and many critical scholars do not accept it as history, and a few (Jane Schaberg) argue that the texts reflect a memory of an irregular birth, a minority view most scholars reject. See the topic The Virgin Birth.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the silenced priest and the singing laity
deep.b:
The chapter is organized around voices. The one man whose office is to speak for God and bless the people, the priest in the sanctuary, is struck silent at the very hour of blessing (1:20–22). Meanwhile people without office speak by the Spirit: an old woman (1:42–45), a young village girl (1:46–55), even an unborn child who "speaks" by leaping (1:41, 44). Zechariah's voice comes back only when he obeys and writes the name God gave, and then he too prophesies by the Spirit (1:64–67).

My suggestion is that Luke is staging, in miniature, what Acts will narrate on a large scale: the Spirit poured out on "men and women" alike, so that God's word is heard outside the sanctuary (Acts 2:17–18), without rejecting the temple or its priests, since the priest's voice is restored and joins the song. Commentators widely note the contrast between Zechariah's doubt and Mary's faith, and the inclusion with Jesus' blessing in 24:50–53; the reading of the chapter as a deliberate transfer and sharing of Israel's voice is my own interpretation.

echoes: Genesis 15:8; Genesis 18:1–15; Judges 13:2–24; 1 Samuel 1:1–2:11; 2 Samuel 6:2–16; 2 Samuel 7:12–16; Isaiah 7:14; Isaiah 9:2–7; Daniel 9:21; Malachi 3:1; Malachi 4:5–6; Psalm 132:11–17; Matthew 1:18–25; Acts 1:1–2

settings.to: Theophilus, a man of rank ("most excellent"), and through him the Gospel's readers
settings.when: At the head of the two-volume work, whenever Luke wrote (the date is debated; see the book introduction)
settings.why: To present the book as a careful, well-ordered account based on eyewitness tradition, so that Theophilus can be sure the teaching he received rests on solid ground. The preface announces that what follows is history in the service of faith, not a collection of rumors.
views: Most scholars: a Christian, perhaps a patron who sponsored the book, who needed assurance about what he had been taught.
Some: an interested outsider or official who had heard reports about the Christians and needed an accurate account (the verb in 1:4 can mean "informed").
A minority, following a suggestion of Origen: "friend of God" stands for every God-loving reader.

settings.to: Zechariah, alone in the sanctuary, while the people pray outside
settings.when: At the hour of the incense offering (morning or evening; many think evening, as in Daniel 9:21), during his division's week of service, in Herod's last years
settings.why: To answer the priest's prayer and Israel's: a son will be born who will prepare Israel for the Lord's coming, in Elijah's spirit, as Malachi promised. The sign of muteness both rebukes Zechariah's doubt and keeps the news hidden until it comes true.
settings.readers: For Luke's readers, many of them Gentiles, the scene shows that the good news begins inside Israel's temple and fulfills Israel's Scriptures; John's followers, who still honored him (Acts 19:1–7), learn that he was sent to prepare for another.

settings.to: Herself and God, in the seclusion of her home
settings.when: In the first months of her pregnancy
settings.why: To give thanks that God has taken away the public shame of her barrenness, in words like Rachel's (Genesis 30:23).

settings.by: The angel Gabriel; Mary's questions and answer
settings.to: Mary, a young virgin promised in marriage to Joseph, in Nazareth
settings.when: In the sixth month of Elizabeth's pregnancy
settings.why: To tell Mary that God has chosen her to bear the Davidic king and Son of God by the power of the Holy Spirit, to answer her question about how it can happen, and to receive her free consent. The scene makes Mary the first to hear the good news about Jesus and the first to believe it.
settings.readers: Luke's readers learn who Jesus is before he is born: David's heir, Son of the Most High, God's Son by the Spirit. Mary's "May it be done to me" models the faith Luke hopes for in Theophilus.
views: Protestant emphasis: Mary is the first disciple who hears God's word and trusts it (1:45; 11:28).
Catholic and Orthodox emphasis: God asks for and receives her free consent; her "yes" is her unique part in the Incarnation (Lumen Gentium 56).

settings.by: Elizabeth, filled with the Holy Spirit
settings.to: Mary, newly arrived at Zechariah's house in the hill country
settings.when: At Mary's greeting, while both are pregnant
settings.why: To recognize, by the Spirit, what no one had told her: that Mary carries "my Lord," and to bless her both for the child and for her faith. Elizabeth's words confirm Gabriel's message to Mary through a second witness.
settings.readers: For Luke's readers the older mother's joy settles the order between John and Jesus, and gives the church the words of blessing it has used ever since.

settings.by: Mary (a few Latin witnesses say Elizabeth; see the variant)
settings.to: God, in the hearing of Elizabeth
settings.when: During Mary's stay with Elizabeth, after Elizabeth's blessing
settings.why: To praise God for choosing a lowly slave woman, and to see in that choice the pattern of his dealings with the world: mercy to those who fear him, the proud scattered, rulers brought down, the hungry fed, and the promise to Abraham kept. The song interprets the coming birth as God's act for all Israel.
settings.readers: Luke's readers, many poor and powerless in the Roman world, heard that God's way runs against the empire's order of honor. The song announces the reversal that runs through the whole Gospel (6:20–26; 16:19–31).
views: Traditional view: Mary composed or spoke it, drawing on the Scriptures she knew.
Many scholars: Luke wrote it in the style of the Greek Old Testament for this setting.
Others: an early Jewish-Christian hymn (Raymond Brown's "Anawim"), or a Jewish victory hymn, adapted by Luke.

settings.by: Zechariah, filled with the Holy Spirit
settings.to: God, and then (1:76–79) the newborn John, before the neighbors and relatives gathered for the circumcision
settings.when: At John's circumcision and naming, on the eighth day, when Zechariah's speech is restored
settings.why: To bless God for raising up a Davidic Savior and keeping his covenant and oath to Abraham, and to tell John his calling: prophet of the Most High, preparing the Lord's way by bringing knowledge of salvation through forgiveness. The song gives the theological meaning of both births.
settings.readers: For Luke's readers the song shows that the Messiah's coming fulfills Israel's covenant hopes, and that John's role is to point beyond himself.
views: Many scholars stress the political language (salvation from enemies) and see a Jewish or Jewish-Christian hymn of national deliverance.
Others stress 1:77: Luke presents salvation as forgiveness and light, reshaping the national hope.

traditions.q: Gabriel greets Mary as kecharitōmenē, "you who have been shown favor" (Latin gratia plena, "full of grace"). Does the greeting teach that Mary was free from sin from the moment of her conception?
views: Yes, the greeting is part of the ground for the dogma of the Immaculate Conception. God prepared Mary to be the mother of the Savior, and the angel salutes her as "full of grace"; she was preserved from all stain of original sin from the first moment of her conception by a singular grace, in view of Christ's merits (Ineffabilis Deus, 1854; Catechism 490–491).

Mary is the All-Holy (Panagia), "full of grace," as the Orthodox greeting "Theotokos and Virgin, rejoice" says, and free from personal sin. But the Orthodox do not accept the 1854 dogma, because they do not hold the Western teaching on inherited guilt that it presupposes; Mary was made holy by the Spirit, above all at the Annunciation.

No. The word means that Mary received God's favor, not that she was a fountain of grace. Luther translated it "you gracious one" (du Holdselige) and defended the choice in his letter On Translating (1530). Luther himself is reported to have still spoken, in a sermon of 1527 for the feast of Mary's conception, of her as preserved from sin, a view he later dropped. Lutheran churches honor Mary as the Mother of God but do not teach the Immaculate Conception.

No. Calvin argued that "full of grace" had been misused to make Mary a source of grace; the angel means she is freely favored by God, as 1:30 explains. Reformed confessions teach that Christ alone was without sin.

The Articles say Christ alone was without sin (Article 15), and the Church of England has never taught the dogma. Anglican opinion is divided: the joint Anglican–Roman Catholic statement of 2005 judged the teaching "consonant with Scripture" in its substance, while many evangelical Anglicans reject it.

No. Mary was a godly woman graciously chosen by God, but a sinner saved by grace like everyone else, who called God "my Savior" (1:47). Grace here is God's favor given, not a quality Mary possessed from her conception. Baptist confessions teach that all humanity, descended from Adam, shares in the sin of our first parents, and make no exception for Mary (Second London Confession 6.2–3).

traditions.q: The angel's and Elizabeth's words (1:28, 42) form the first half of the Hail Mary, and Mary says every generation will call her blessed (1:48). Should Christians pray the Hail Mary and ask Mary to pray for them?
views: Yes. The Hail Mary joins the angel's greeting and Elizabeth's blessing to a petition, "Holy Mary, Mother of God, pray for us sinners, now and at the hour of our death." Asking Mary's intercession honors Christ, the one mediator, whose mother shares in his work by her prayer (Catechism 2676–2679; Lumen Gentium 60–62).
Yes. Orthodox worship greets her daily, "Theotokos and Virgin, rejoice," and asks her prayers in nearly every service: "Most Holy Theotokos, save us," meaning by her intercession with her Son.

The angel's greeting may be used as praise of God's grace to Mary, as Luther explained it in his Personal Prayer Book (1522), but Lutherans do not invoke Mary or the saints. The Augsburg Confession (21) says Scripture teaches us to honor the saints and imitate their faith, not to call on them, since Christ is our only mediator.

No. Religious worship and prayer are to be given to God alone, through Christ alone, "not to angels, saints, or any other creature" (Westminster Confession 21.2). Mary is honored as blessed by imitating her faith, not by addressing prayers to her.

The Articles reject the "invocation of saints" as without warrant in Scripture (Article 22). Practice is divided: Anglo-Catholics pray the Hail Mary and the Angelus, while evangelical Anglicans do not.

No. There is "one mediator between God and humans" (1 Timothy 2:5); Christians honor Mary as blessed by remembering her faith, and pray to God alone. The Second London Confession (22.2) repeats the Westminster wording.

title: Born in David's town
sum: Caesar Augustus orders a registration, and Joseph goes from Nazareth to Bethlehem, David's town, with Mary, who is pregnant. There she gives birth to her firstborn son and lays him in a manger, because the guest room has no space. An angel announces to shepherds in the fields "a Savior ... who is Messiah and Lord," and an army of angels sings of glory to God and peace on earth. The shepherds find the child and tell what they heard, and Mary treasures it all.

Jesus is circumcised and named on the eighth day. After forty days his parents bring him to the temple, keeping the law of Moses, with the poor family's offering. The devout Simeon takes him in his arms and sings that he can now die in peace, for he has seen God's salvation, a light for the nations and glory for Israel; he warns Mary of a sword. The aged prophetess Anna gives thanks and speaks of him. Twelve years later, at Passover, the boy Jesus stays behind in the temple among the teachers, and when his parents find him he says he must be at his Father's. He returns to Nazareth, obedient, and grows in wisdom and favor.
readings: Traditional readers take the chapter as historical, though they disagree about how to fit the census of Quirinius to Herod's reign (see the deep dive). They point to the ordinary details: swaddling, the poor family's offering, the yearly pilgrimage, the caravan, the temple teachers. Critical historians usually accept that Jesus grew up in Nazareth, was born to Mary and Joseph near the end of Herod's reign, and was raised in an observant family, but doubt the census as Luke describes it and see the angels and songs as theological storytelling.

Luke sets the birth in the reign of Augustus, the ruler Greek cities hailed as savior and bringer of peace, whose birthday was called "good news." Luke's angel uses the same words, savior, good news, peace, for a baby in a feeding trough. Without any call to revolt, the story quietly relocates the world's true Lord and true peace.

Luke's Gospel begins and ends in the temple. Here Jesus is brought to the temple as a baby, welcomed by a righteous man and a prophetess who represent faithful Israel, and returns at twelve to sit among its teachers, calling it his Father's house. Jesus' life is framed by Israel's holiest place, which he will cleanse and in which he will teach daily (19:45–47).

views.H: The chapter names Augustus and Quirinius and dates the birth by a census, the best-known historical difficulty in Luke (see the deep dive). Other details fit what is known: Roman provincial censuses for taxation, travel to ancestral or property towns in Egyptian practice, village houses with animals inside, the offering of the poor (Leviticus 12:8), pilgrimage caravans and teachers in the temple courts.
views.C: On the majority view that Luke did not know Matthew, the two tell independent birth stories that agree on key points (Herod's reign, Mary and Joseph, a virginal conception, Bethlehem, a home in Nazareth) and differ on most others: Luke has no magi, star, massacre or flight to Egypt; Matthew has no census, shepherds or presentation. Most critical scholars think each evangelist used different traditions and shaped them by theme. Luke's chronology (census under Quirinius) is widely judged inaccurate; conservative scholars propose ways to reconcile it.
views.L: Luke contrasts power and humility: Augustus orders the world, and a baby lies in a manger; an army of angels sings of peace. The chapter is shaped by threes: the angel, the shepherds and Mary's pondering; Simeon and Anna, a man and a woman; and the frame of growth (2:40, 52). Mary "turning them over in her heart" (2:19, 51) brackets the chapter's second half. Jesus' first words (2:49) already state his identity ("my Father") and his necessity ("I must").
views.J: Luke stresses five times that the family did all the law required (2:22–24, 27, 39), and he presents Simeon and Anna as faithful Jews awaiting Israel's comfort and Jerusalem's redemption. The boy Jesus sits among Jewish teachers as a learner and questioner. Jewish scholars note that Luke presents Jesus' Judaism without embarrassment, and that later Christian readings that set Jesus against "the law" find no support here.
views.T: From this chapter come Christmas (December 25 in the West, January 6 in some Eastern traditions), the Gloria, the Feast of the Circumcision or Holy Name (January 1), the Presentation or Meeting of the Lord and Candlemas (February 2), the Nunc Dimittis at Compline, and the Finding in the Temple, one of the Joyful Mysteries of the rosary. The manger scene was popularized by Francis of Assisi at Greccio in 1223. Simeon's "sword" shaped devotion to Our Lady of Sorrows.

deep.h: The census under Quirinius: the evidence
deep.b:
Luke 2:1–2 dates Jesus' birth by a registration ordered by Augustus, "the first such registration, carried out while Quirinius governed Syria." Three facts make this hard:

1. Herod. Luke (1:5) and Matthew (2:1) agree that Jesus was born while Herod the Great was king. Herod is usually dated to have died in 4 BC (a minority argues for 1 BC).

2. Quirinius. Publius Sulpicius Quirinius was governor (legate) of Syria from AD 6. Josephus reports that in that year, after Archelaus was removed, Quirinius took a census of Judea, now under direct Roman rule, which caused the revolt of Judas the Galilean (Antiquities 18.1–4, 26; Acts 5:37). Known governors of Syria in the last years of Herod were Sentius Saturninus (about 9–6 BC) and Quinctilius Varus (about 6–4 BC).

3. A Roman census in Herod's kingdom. Herod was an allied king who collected his own taxes; a direct Roman census of his subjects during his reign would be unusual, though Rome could demand information from client kings.

Proposed solutions: Luke confused the census of AD 6 with the time of Jesus' birth (most critical scholars); Quirinius held an earlier command in the region, perhaps a military one, and an inscription from Tivoli may refer to a governor of Syria serving "a second time" (William Ramsay and others, though the inscription does not name him); prōtē means "before" ("this registration happened before Quirinius governed Syria"); a registration or oath of loyalty in Herod's last years (Josephus, Antiquities 17.42) was later remembered by the better-known name; or the early date given by Tertullian (Against Marcion 4.19), that the census was taken under Sentius Saturninus, preserves a correct tradition. None has won general agreement. Justin Martyr told the emperor that the census records could be checked (First Apology 34), but no such records survive.

Agreements: Herod's reign, Mary and Joseph promised but not yet living together, Joseph of David's line, the conception by the Holy Spirit without a human father, the angelic command to name him Jesus, birth in Bethlehem, a home in Nazareth. On the majority view that Luke did not know Matthew, these shared points are older than both; on the Farrer view, Luke knew Matthew's story and retold it. Harmonizers place the magi and Egypt after Luke 2:38; critical scholars think the two accounts cannot be fully combined.

deep.title: Claude's theory: two registrations
deep.b:
Luke uses the word apographē, "registration," only twice: here (2:2) and in Acts 5:37, where Gamaliel recalls that "Judas the Galilean appeared at the time of the registration" and led people into revolt. Luke's readers who knew Josephus' story, or the memory of it, knew that the registration was the moment the movement of armed resistance to Rome was born.

My suggestion is that Luke deliberately sets Joseph and Mary on the other side of that line: the royal family of David obeys the emperor's order, travels to be counted, and the Messiah is born in the course of that obedience. For Theophilus, a man of rank in the empire, this would say that the movement around Jesus is not Judas the Galilean's, even though it proclaims a Savior, peace and a king. Many scholars have argued that Luke-Acts has a political apologetic toward Rome (Hans Conzelmann is the best known); the specific link between the two "registrations" as a contrast between Jesus' family and Judas the Galilean is my own reading, and it does not depend on solving the historical problem of the date.

echoes: Micah 5:2; Isaiah 1:3; Isaiah 7:14; Isaiah 9:6–7; Isaiah 40:1–5; Isaiah 49:6; Isaiah 52:9–10; Exodus 13:2; Exodus 13:12–15; Leviticus 12:1–8; 1 Samuel 1:22–28; 1 Samuel 2:20–26; Matthew 1:18–2:23; Acts 5:37; Acts 28:28

settings.by: Caesar Augustus, through his provincial governor
settings.to: The subjects of the empire, here the people of Judea and Galilee
settings.when: In Herod's last years, on Luke's dating; Luke links it to Quirinius' governorship of Syria
settings.why: A Roman registration listed people and property for taxation. It bound every head of household in the region it covered and required him to be entered on the rolls; in Egyptian practice people went to their home district to be registered. In the story it moves Joseph to David's town at the right time.
settings.readers: For Luke's readers the decree sets the world's ruler and the newborn king side by side; and it shows Jesus' family obeying Rome, not resisting it.
views: Conservative scholars: a registration in Herod's last years, perhaps connected with Quirinius in an earlier role.
Most critical scholars: Luke joined the birth to the census of AD 6 that Josephus describes.

settings.what: The angel's announcement to the shepherds
settings.to: Shepherds keeping night watch over their flock in the fields near Bethlehem
settings.why: To announce the birth as good news of great joy for all Israel, to name the child Savior, Messiah and Lord, and to give the shepherds a sign by which to find him. The first hearers of the Messiah's birth are working people in the fields, not rulers or priests.
settings.readers: Luke's readers heard the vocabulary of imperial announcements (good news, savior, peace) applied to a child in a manger, and the promise that the lowly are the first to hear (1:52).

settings.by: A crowd of heaven's army, with the angel
settings.to: God, in the hearing of the shepherds
settings.why: To give glory to God and declare peace on earth for those God favors: the birth is heaven's victory celebration, and its fruit is peace.
settings.readers: For readers living under the "peace of Augustus" kept by legions, the song declared a different peace, from God.

settings.what: The laws of purification and of the firstborn
settings.by: The law of Moses (Leviticus 12:2–8; Exodus 13:2, 12–15), as Luke summarizes it
settings.to: Mary and Joseph, as an Israelite mother and father
settings.when: Forty days after the birth, at the temple in Jerusalem
settings.why: Leviticus 12 binds a woman after childbirth: after forty days for a son she brings a burnt offering and a sin offering, two birds if she cannot afford a lamb, and is declared clean so that she may again touch holy things and enter the sanctuary. Exodus 13 claims every firstborn son for God, to be redeemed, in memory of the exodus. Both applied to every Israelite family; Luke shows Jesus' family keeping them faithfully.
settings.readers: For Gentile readers Luke explains that Jesus came from a family faithful to Israel's law, and that his first public appearance was in God's temple. The poor family's offering shows the humility of his birth.

settings.by: Simeon, a righteous and devout man of Jerusalem, moved by the Spirit
settings.to: God ("Master"), with the child in his arms, before Mary and Joseph
settings.when: At the presentation in the temple
settings.why: To thank God for keeping his promise that Simeon would see the Lord's Messiah before he died, and to declare that this child is God's salvation, prepared before all peoples: light for the nations and glory for Israel. The song widens the hope of chapter 1 from Israel to the whole world.
settings.readers: For Luke's largely Gentile readers, the song promises them a place in Israel's salvation, without taking Israel's glory away; it anticipates the mission of Acts (Acts 13:47; 28:28).

settings.when: After his song, as he blesses the parents
settings.why: To warn that the child will divide Israel, a sign that will be opposed, causing many to fall and rise, and that Mary herself will suffer: a sword will go through her soul. The joyful birth stories turn here toward the cross.
settings.readers: Luke's readers knew that Jesus had been rejected by many and that his followers were "spoken against everywhere" (Acts 28:22); Simeon's words show that this division was foreseen.

settings.by: Anna, a widowed prophetess of the tribe of Asher
settings.to: God, and then everyone in the temple who was looking for Jerusalem's redemption
settings.when: At the same hour as Simeon's words
settings.why: To give thanks to God and to tell those who shared Israel's hope that its redemption had come. Luke gives no words, but presents her as the first to speak about Jesus to others in Jerusalem.
settings.readers: With Simeon she forms a pair, a man and a woman, as Luke often pairs stories; some see a deliberate double witness (Deuteronomy 19:15). Luke's readers see faithful Jewish men and women welcoming Jesus first.

settings.what: The law of the pilgrimage feasts
settings.to: Every Israelite male, three times a year; families in practice
settings.why: The law required men to appear before the LORD at the three pilgrimage feasts; by Jesus' time many families from Galilee went at least for Passover, with women and children. The scene shows the family's faithfulness and brings the twelve-year-old Jesus to the temple.

settings.what: Mary's question and Jesus' first words
settings.when: In the temple after three days of searching
settings.why: Mary's reproach is a mother's distress. Jesus' answer, the first words he speaks in Luke, gently corrects "your father" with "my Father" and states that he "must" be in his Father's house or about his Father's affairs. His parents do not understand.
settings.readers: Luke's readers hear Jesus himself, before his public work, claim God as Father and the temple as his Father's house, and see that even his family understood him only slowly.

traditions.q: Luke tells of Jesus' birth (2:1–20), but the Bible gives no date and no command to celebrate it. Should Christians keep Christmas as a holy day?
views: Yes. The Nativity of the Lord is one of the principal feasts of the church year, a holy day of obligation, with its own season from Christmas to the Baptism of the Lord. The church may set feasts that celebrate the mysteries of Christ.
Yes. The Nativity is one of the Great Feasts, prepared for by a forty-day fast. Churches that keep the old Julian calendar celebrate December 25 on what is January 7 in the civil calendar.
Yes. Lutherans keep the church year, and the Augsburg Confession (15) approves holy days and feasts that serve good order and teaching, as long as they are not made necessary for salvation.
Yes. The Book of Common Prayer appoints Christmas Day with its own collect and readings, and the church year is kept.

Historically divided. The Westminster Assembly's Directory for Public Worship (1645) taught that only the Lord's Day is commanded and that festival days "having no warrant in the word of God" should not be kept, and Puritan New England for a time banned Christmas celebrations. Most Reformed and Presbyterian churches today keep Christmas; some strict Presbyterian bodies still do not.

No. Witnesses do not celebrate Christmas, because the Bible gives no date or command, because they hold its customs to come from pagan festivals, and because they do not celebrate birthdays. They keep only the yearly Memorial of Christ's death.
